source_refs.note: Topic 29.6.2 with Examples 29.4 and 29.5, Table 29.3 and Quick Check 29.3, answered (PDF 196-199). Table 29.3 lists C6H13+ 85 while the text uses C6H14+ 86 for M; both are kept. The ionisation equation is given in full. Exercises (PDF 199-201) excluded; answers need review.

blocks.text: When molecules are bombarded with fast electrons they lose an electron, forming a positively charged molecular ion with one unpaired electron: molecule + e- -> molecule.+ + 2e-. The molecular ion can break up further into new ions, molecules and free radicals.

Each peak corresponds to an ion of a particular m/e. The peak with the highest m/e is usually the molecular ion (M+) peak, which gives the molecular mass of the compound. In Example 29.4 the molecular ion peak is at m/e 58, so the spectrum belongs to propanal, CH3CH2CHO (Mr 58), not butanal, CH3CH2CH2CHO (Mr 72).

Different compounds can have the same molecular mass, so fragmentation helps to find the structure. Fragments appear as smaller characteristic ions or from the loss of small molecules, giving peaks at, for example, 18 (H2O), 29 (C2H5+) and 44 (CO2). Simple alkanes break at their C-C bonds: straight-chain hexane gives peaks at 86 (C6H14+), 71 (C5H11+), 57 (C4H9+), 43 (C3H7+), 29 (C2H5+) and 15 (CH3+).
c) The M+1 and M+2 peaks

The M+1 peak is caused by carbon-13 in the molecule. About 1.1% of all carbon atoms are 13C, so the M+1 peak is much smaller than the M peak, and the more carbon atoms a molecule has, the taller its M+1 peak (hexane's M+1 peak is relatively larger than ethane's). The number of carbon atoms, n, is n = (100 x abundance of M+1) / (1.1 x abundance of M+). In Example 29.5 the M peak at m/e 58 has abundance about 85 and the M+1 peak at 59 has abundance 3, so n = (100 x 3) / (1.1 x 85) = 3.21, that is three carbon atoms.

Bromine and chlorine atoms give an M+2 (and possibly an M+4) peak. Chlorine exists as 35Cl and 37Cl in a 3:1 ratio, so a compound with one Cl atom shows M and M+2 peaks in the ratio 3:1, and one with two Cl atoms shows M, M+2 and M+4 in the ratio 9:6:1. Bromine exists as 79Br and 81Br in almost equal amounts, so one Br atom gives M and M+2 peaks of equal height (1:1), and two Br atoms give M, M+2 and M+4 in the ratio 1:2:1.

blocks.alt: Top: the mass spectrum of boron, bars at m/e 10 (19.9%) and 11 (80.1%), with Ar = (19.9 x 10 + 80.1 x 11)/100 = 10.80. Below, four stick patterns: one Cl, peaks at 35 and 37 in the ratio 3:1; two Cl, peaks at 70, 72 and 74 in 9:6:1; one Br, peaks at 79 and 81 in 1:1; two Br, peaks at 158, 160 and 162 in 1:2:1.
blocks.caption: Isotope peaks of boron, chlorine and bromine (original stick spectra after the book's mass spectra).
blocks.long_description: Each isotope gives its own peak, and the peak heights follow the natural abundances. Chlorine (35 and 37 in 3:1) and bromine (79 and 81 in about 1:1) therefore give their compounds characteristic groups of peaks two mass units apart.

blocks.alt: Top: the fragments of hexane with their m/e values: C6H14+ 86 (molecular ion), C5H11+ 71, C4H9+ 57, C3H7+ 43, C2H5+ 29 and CH3+ 15, each differing by CH2 (14). Bottom: the mass spectrum of CH3Br from Quick Check 29.3, sticks at m/e 15 (CH3+), 94 (CH3 79Br+) and 96 (CH3 81Br+), heights as drawn in the book.
blocks.caption: Fragments of hexane and the mass spectrum of bromomethane (original diagram after Table 29.3 and Quick Check 29.3).
blocks.long_description: Breaking a C-C bond in hexane can leave any of the alkyl cations, so the spectrum shows a family of peaks 14 apart. Bromomethane shows its molecular ions at 94 and 96, one for each bromine isotope, in almost equal heights, and a CH3+ fragment at 15 from the loss of a bromine atom.

items: Give the possible fragments (as straight-chain alkanes) of (i) C4H10, (ii) C5H12, (iii) C7H16.
The mass spectrum of CH3Br has peaks at 15, 94 and 96. Identify each, and explain why there are two peaks at 94 and 96.
